newsitem.title: GERMANY: SPD barons may open way to German tax deal.
newsitem.headline: SPD barons may open way to German tax deal.

text.p: After the collapse of talks on tax reforms last week, German opposition leaders have begun cautiously looking for ways to break the political logjam that has become the latest point of discord in deadlocked Bonn.
Recent comments by some Social Democrat (SPD) state leaders indicate they do not stand four-square behind the hard line on taxes that their chairman Oskar Lafontaine has decreed.

The party's line on Chancellor Helmut Kohl's planned tax reform, an issue it can block thanks to its majority in the upper house of parliament, is still unclear but a trend towards a compromise this autumn seemed to be taking shape.

Hamburg Mayor Henning Voscherau said on Tuesday the SPD had to agree to slash the top personal tax rate from 53 percent, a Kohl plan Lafontaine has denounced in what sound like premature campaign speeches for next year's general election.
"We have no choice but to come to an agreement on the peak rate," he told ARD television.
This pragmatic approach echoed comments by Lower Saxony state premier Gerhard Schroeder, Lafontaine's main rival for the privilege of running against Kohl in the October poll.
"Sometimes it is overlooked that there are great problems with the tax reform, but we have to try to reach a compromise," Schroeder said on Monday.

Other SPD state premiers like Heide Simonis in Schleswig- Holstein and Kurt Beck from Rhineland-Palatinate have also raised eyebrows by stressing the need to compromise rather than the all-out opposition that would fit Lafontaine's stragegy.

At the same time Schroeder, seen by the press as the leader of the more moderate state premiers, has stressed the states would not let Bonn play divide and conquer by driving a wedge between them and the national SPD leadership.

Politicians earned a stinging rebuke from President Roman Herzog at the weekend for indulging in a political blockade which he said was thwarting reforms to boost growth and cut unemployment now standing at 4.5 million.
Schroeder responded: "The President has the right to state his views on political problems. Everyone must reflect on that -- the SPD too."

Commentators have said Lafontaine's tough tax stand was to blame for the failure of the talks. But Lafontaine has showed no sign of backing down, saying government legislation had "no chance because it cannot be financed".

"The states will make their contribution to wipe away this impression that politicians in Bonn are immobile," Rhineland- Palatinate premier Beck told German TV on Monday night. "We will be constructive...but the government must take the lead."

Lafontaine moved at the weekend to get the party to back his refusal to cut the top rate of income tax. In a letter to SPD functionaries he said that the party could not agree to "tax giveaways to the rich".
Leaders in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition have zeroed in on the divergence in views between the SPD state premiers and Lafontaine as reopening the chance of a tax deal.

Guido Westerwelle, general secretary of junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP), said: "I have the impression that more and more SPD state premiers are fulfilling their oath of office to their states, and not to Oskar Lafontaine."

The emerging differences between Lafontaine -- who is also premier in the tiny Saarland state on the French border -- and regional chiefs on tax could open into a rift which could end up deciding who ends up leading the party into the 1998 vote.
Schroeder -- a pragmatic moderate compared by many German commentators to Britain's Tony Blair -- could get a big boost if Labour wins by a healthy margin at this Thursday's election.
The pro-business Schroeder has also been riding high in recent opinion polls -- which show that he would beat Kohl in a head-to-head direct vote, while Lafontaine would lose.

Sixty-eight percent of those surveyed by the Emnid research group for this week's Spiegel news weekly said they would like to see Schroeder playing an important role in Germany's future, a rise of nine points on the previous poll.

Kohl was stable on 45 percent, while Lafontaine's rating fell eight points to 44 percent after the collapse of the tax talks. "Confidence in parties and politicians has fallen...only Schroeder could collect plus points," Spiegel wrote.
